title: Jewish students say antisemitism normalised at UK universities
description: Like many campuses across the UK, Cardiff University has seen pro-Palestine protests in recent years and Oliver said he believed some behaviour he wit
body: Like many campuses across the UK, Cardiff University has seen pro-Palestine protests in recent years and Oliver said he believed some behaviour he witnessed crossed the line from criticism of Israel into antisemitism.Holding Jewish people responsible for the actions of the Israeli government is a form of antisemitism, according to the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance."That first year was absolutely terrifying," he said."You go home and think, 'do I carry on? Do I try to go to the next day?'"Oliver said he stopped speaking Hebrew outside his home, and hid his Star of David pendant when on campus.Over the following three years, Oliver said the antisemitic abuse he experienced at university became "relentless"."I've been in clubs [or] just wandering around the uni and you hear these conversations and you see pamphlets being handed around where it's literally saying that your belief and your history is fake," he said."I've been at house parties where, when someone's found out I'm Jewish they started calling me Netanyahu behind my back."Like you found out my religion and you've decided I'm a bad person."Oliver said when he had reported antisemitic incidents that had happened to him and others, he had felt they had been often "swept under the rug" by the university.Although he said some positive action had been taken, he feels more needs to be done.Cardiff University said it was sorry that "any student felt unsafe" on campus and that it adopts a "zero-tolerance approach to harassment and discrimination of all kinds".It said there was no place for antisemitism or hatred at the university and they have "robust procedures" in place for investigating allegations of antisemitism. Where it is found, the university said appropriate action would be taken.It said it had reached out to the university's Jewish Society and reminded students to report incidents to them.Daniel, the incoming Jewish Society vice-president at Manchester University, said Jewish students in the city had started "hiding their identity" after the 7 October attacks and later the Heaton Park attack in October 2025, when two Jewish people were killed after a car was driven into pedestrians outside a synagogue.He said antisemitic slogans and swastikas had been daubed on walls and a swastika drawn on a fridge at a house party after partygoers had discovered the host was Jewish. Daniel said he was aware a Jewish student wearing a kippah had also been warned by staff not to enter an academic building during protests for fear of their safety."To be Jewish at university is to have an identity that is inherently politicised by everyone around you," he said. "That becomes very exhausting because it's a very difficult place to navigate."A University of Manchester spokesperson said previous incidents of offensive graffiti on campus were removed promptly, with involvement from police.They said the unversity took antisemitism "extremely seriously" and investigated it, and that the university has worked closely with civic and faith leaders to promote dialogue and understanding between communities.They added: "We are working with Jewish students, staff and community representatives to strengthen our response to antisemitism."There is however more to do, and we are working with the Antisemitism Policy Trust and other universities to share learning, identify effective practice and strengthen our collective response to antisemitism."The president of Swansea University's Jewish Society said she had to alert local counter-terrorism officers when organising routine activities for the society."I don't think anyone running, say, the Manga [Japanese comic books] Society has to consider whether there's a hate crime risk from having a stall," said Aviva."I'm a 20-year-old just going about university life. Getting calls from the police to tell me there isn't a terrorism risk isn't a normal experience."Swansea University said it supports students through dedicated wellbeing, academic and faith services, and is maintaining a zero-tolerance approach to harassment and discrimination.A recent survey, external of 1,000 students commissioned by the Union of Jewish Students, conducted by JL Partners between January and February 2026, said Jewish students were being "isolated by their peers" because of the Israel-Palestine conflict. The poll suggested "apathy" towards antisemitism, with one in four (25%) students saying they did not care "very much" or "at all" if students are able to be open about their Jewish identity.

schema.headline: Jewish students say antisemitism normalised at UK universities

title: Netanyahu accuses NYC's Mamdani of 'fomenting hate' after arrest threat
description: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he planned to attend the UN General Assembly in New York City this autumn, despite the city's mayor, Zo
body: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he planned to attend the UN General Assembly in New York City this autumn, despite the city's mayor, Zohran Mamdani, making threats to arrest him.Mamdani walked back that threat last week, acknowledging he lacked the legal power to arrest Netanyahu on a warrant issued by the International Criminal Court, the world's top war-crimes court. The Israeli leader told Fox News on Sunday that he was "not concerned" about Mamdani's previous pledge and accused the mayor of "fomenting hate"."He's supposed to be the mayor of all New Yorkers, Jews, Christians, Muslims, everyone, but he's trying to turn one group against the other," Netanyahu said.Netanyahu referenced a pair of stabbings in New York on Thursday, in which a suspect stabbed a Jewish man and an Asian man just blocks apart.The suspect allegedly shouted the phrase "Allahu akbar" while committing the stabbings, according to police. He has been charged with hate crimes relating to each victim.Both men survived the attacks, which drew condemnations from the city's Jewish and Asian American leaders.In the aftermath, Netanyahu said Jewish New Yorkers were "afraid right now."The mayor's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.Mamdani, a staunch supporter of Palestinian rights, made his opposition to the Israeli military operation in Gaza a central plank of his campaign last year. In an address last week, he called Netanyahu a "war criminal."As part of that platform while campaigning, Mamdani promised to enforce a 2024 arrest warrant for Netanyahu from the International Criminal Court (ICC), which accused the prime minister of committing war crimes in Gaza.Israel has denied charges that it has committed war crimes in Gaza, and Netanyahu called the charges "bogus".The Israeli military entered Gaza after the Hamas-led attack in Israel on 7 October 2023. About 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage.Over 73,000 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since then, including more than 21,000 children, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.Last week, after the New York Times pressed Mamdani on his pledge to arrest Netanyahu, Mamdani said his administration had reviewed the law and found: "We do not have the independent legal authority to enforce this warrant".Mamdani urged the federal government to arrest the prime minister, and said: "Benjamin Netanyahu is not welcome in New York City."

schema.headline: Netanyahu accuses NYC's Mamdani of 'fomenting hate' after arrest threat

title: Andy Burnham tells BBC NHS 'will collapse' without social care reform
description: Andy Burnham has told the BBC "the NHS will collapse" if social care is not reformed but said he could not put a timeline on changes.In his first majo
body: Andy Burnham has told the BBC "the NHS will collapse" if social care is not reformed but said he could not put a timeline on changes.In his first major interview since becoming prime minister, Burnham said he would not want to leave office without bringing in "substantial change" to the social care system.The prime minister also suggested making it harder to claim benefits, saying the country had to get serious about getting the welfare bill down.Kemi Badenoch has meanwhile written to the prime minister, saying he should rule out tax rises or increased borrowing to fund social care reform.In his interview with the BBC, Burnham said if the government did not reform social care, the NHS would "collapse under the weight of trying to care for people who've really not needed to end up in the NHS system".But pressed on whether he would create a new system before the next election, he said he "couldn't put a timeline on it right here, right now", though he would put "whatever political capital I have into fixing broken social care".Burnham first proposed a universal system of social care in England in 2009 when he was health secretary under Gordon Brown.Now as prime minister he is due to make a speech on adult social care on Wednesday.The BBC understands the PM will stop short of unveiling plans for a new system in this speech, instead announcing he is speeding up the Casey Commission, an independent review which has been considering possible solutions for social care.Currently Baroness Louise Casey is not expected to give her final recommendations until 2028, but Burnham wants to bring her schedule forward.He told the BBC: "Social care was on longer path and I have brought it straight forward."Adult social care provides support to help people live more independently, ranging from personal care such as washing to household tasks.Unlike the NHS, social care is not free at the point of use. In England and Northern Ireland people with savings worth more than £23,250 are not entitled to help with care costs from their council.In Wales and Scotland different rules apply in terms of eligibility.Adult social care has proved a complex issue to tackle for successive governments.Two years ago Sir Keir Starmer was criticised when Labour scrapped plans for an £86,000 cap on the amount people in England would spend on social care in their lifetime.Conservative leader Badenoch wrote in her letter to Burnham that "any solution to the issues around social care must also be fair to those who have made provisions and saved up over the course of their lives".

schema.headline: Andy Burnham tells BBC NHS 'will collapse' without social care reform

title: Trump paused attacks on Iran to make space for talks, US ambassador says
description: President Donald Trump has paused attacks on Iran for the second night in a row to give diplomacy more time, the US ambassador to the UN said.Speaking
body: President Donald Trump has paused attacks on Iran for the second night in a row to give diplomacy more time, the US ambassador to the UN said.Speaking to Fox News on Sunday, ambassador Mike Waltz said the president was "giving talks some space, he's giving it a little bit of room".An Iranian army spokesperson said on Sunday that Tehran had halted "retaliatory" attacks in the region in response.The pause follows nearly two weeks of daily US strikes and tit-for-tat attacks, effectively unravelling the ceasefire struck in June.Asked whether Trump had decided against escalation for now, Waltz told NBC: "I wouldn't go that far at all. The president is keeping all options on the table."Waltz also rejected reports in the New York Times, external that administration officials had warned expanding hostilities could dangerously drain a diminished stockpile of air defence munitions."The US military... has everything that it needs to conduct this campaign as effectively as it needs to be," he said.As of Sunday evening, Trump had not spoken publicly on the latest developments, but earlier posted computer-generated images on his Truth Social account that depicted US military planes bombing Iranian ships and Kharg island.Meanwhile, Iran and Oman held several rounds of technical talks in Tehran on Friday and Saturday to discuss management of the Strait of Hormuz, according to Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei. Disputes over control of the strait reignited US-Iran tensions earlier this month and it remains a major block to permanently ending the war.Iran and the US signed a memorandum of understanding in June to halt military operations and reopen the strait, as well as to reach an agreement to end the war over the following 60 days.But after Iranian forces attacked tankers in the Strait of Hormuz on 13 July, the US resumed airstrikes on the country and reinstated its naval blockade on Iranian ports.Iran retaliated with attacks on US military facilities and bases across the Middle East, killing four American soldiers. The US strikes have since killed dozens of people, according to Iran's health ministry.In the UK, new Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said he would meet his US counterpart Pete Hegseth in the coming week to discuss the strait, which is one of the world's key transport routes for oil, liquid natural gas and other essential commodities. "When it comes to securing maritime freedom and free commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, that's where we are absolutely aligned," Streeting told the BBC.Earlier this week, oil prices hit $100 a barrel for the first time since May, as the renewed fighting stoked fears over global energy supplies.As the war nears its fifth month, it remains largely unpopular in the US, with a new poll from CBS/YouGov suggesting 57% of Americans are frustrated about the conflict and only 19% optimistic.Thousands of people have been killed across the Middle East since the US-Israeli war with Iran began in February, official figures show, with the vast majority coming from Iran and Lebanon.President Trump is set to meet Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the White House on Tuesday.

schema.headline: Trump paused attacks on Iran to make space for talks, US ambassador says

title: The Hundred 2026 results: Trent Rockets beat London Spirit
description: The Hundred men's competition, Trent BridgeLondon Spirit 159-9 (100 balls): Brevis 39 (24); Harrison 2-25Trent Rockets 160-6 (98 balls): Duckett 75 (4
body: The Hundred men's competition, Trent BridgeLondon Spirit 159-9 (100 balls): Brevis 39 (24); Harrison 2-25Trent Rockets 160-6 (98 balls): Duckett 75 (47); Milne 2-25Trent Rockets won by four wickets ScorecardCraig Overton won an entertaining contest against twin brother Jamie as Trent Rockets edged a thriller by four wickets against London Spirit in the men's Hundred.The home side's chase of 160 in Nottingham went down to the wire with 10 needed off five balls, but Craig audaciously ramped for six before calmly ticking off the remaining runs with two deliveries to spare.He finished unbeaten on 20 from only six balls as Rockets earned their first win of this year's tournament."He got me out last year so I had to get some payback," Craig told BBC Sport."It's still a bit weird playing against each other. We're getting used to it after a few years."We're both very competitive - we both always want to win - so I think the family will be happy with how we played it." Rockets' chase was set up by Ben Duckett's 75 from 47 balls at the top of the order, an innings which included 12 fours and two sixes and led an impressive recovery after he lost his opening partner Finn Allen for a duck.Duckett fell with 52 runs needed from 26 balls, which looked to have swung momentum Sprit's way, but Sam Billings' 22 off 10 combined with Overton's knock got them over the line.The Hundred men's competition, Emirates Old TraffordManchester Super Giants 187-5 (100 balls): Buttler 90 (50); Rehan 2-43Birmingham Phoenix 100 all out (97 balls): Ferreira 23 (25); Dawson 3-15Manchester Super Giants won by 87 runsScorecard. TableJos Buttler produced a masterful 90 from 50 balls as Manchester Super Giants demolished Birmingham Phoenix by 87 runs to maintain their perfect start to The Hundred.After making his highest T20 score of 131 against India this month, the England wicketkeeper-batter continued his resurgence, striking seven fours and five sixes to lead the home side to 187-5.It was the second highest Hundred total at Old Trafford and one that Phoenix fell well short of as they were bundled out for 100, handing Super Giants their second win in two matches.The women's fixture was washed out and the men's game delayed by 30 minutes but, once the action got under way, fans were treated to a sensational innings from Buttler.Super Giants suffered early setbacks as Tim Seifert and captain Aiden Markram fell cheaply, but Buttler combined power-hitting with deft touches around the ground to bring up his half-century in 31 balls.Buttler's superb innings came to end with three balls remaining, while Tom Moores added an unbeaten 39 from 17 deliveries.

schema.headline: The Hundred 2026 results: Trent Rockets beat London Spirit

title: Andy Burnham pledges continued support for Ukraine ahead of Zelensky visit
description: Andy Burnham has pledged to continue the UK's "unwavering" support for Ukraine ahead of meeting Volodymyr Zelensky on Monday.The Ukrainian president w
body: Andy Burnham has pledged to continue the UK's "unwavering" support for Ukraine ahead of meeting Volodymyr Zelensky on Monday.The Ukrainian president will become the prime minister's first international visitor since he took office a week ago, which No 10 said "illustrates the strength of the relationship between the two nations".They will visit a naval base, where Burnham will announce the sharing of the intellectual property behind the UK's new "Stone Cloak" electronic warfare system, enabling Ukraine to produce the technology at scale.Burnham told the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg ahead of the visit that he was looking forward to it and that his support for Ukraine was "unwavering - it is 100%".The Stone Cloak jammers are the size of a tablet computer and are designed to block the detection of any drones they are fitted to.The Ministry of Defence has already given thousands of the devices to Ukrainian forces to bolster their drone operations.Downing Street said that following its deployment in Ukraine, the technology will be built into the UK's next generation of long-range weapons.It said this would include Project Brakestop, a government programme to develop low-cost cruise missiles - self-propelled guided weapons that fly like normal aircraft for much of their flight.Burnham said in a statement on Sunday evening: "Stone Cloak is the best of homegrown British innovation and proven on the frontline, and it will be vital to protecting our security in both our countries."During Monday's visit, the two leaders will also meet more than 200 Ukrainian military personnel who have spent the last three weeks taking part in a maritime exercise in the UK.Exercise Sea Breeze is aimed at strengthening warfighting capabilities and counter-mine measures in the Black Sea.Britain's backing of Ukraine has been constant since Russia's invasion four years ago, and the UK has committed £25bn in funding, external for the country's warfighting efforts.In one of his first calls after becoming prime minister last Monday, Burnham spoke to Zelensky and invited him to visit the UK "at the earliest opportunity".Zelensky wrote on X shortly afterwards: "I truly appreciate that the support for Ukraine and our people will remain steadfast."Burnham's predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, visited Kyiv on his final full day as Labour leader.During that trip, he announced fresh funding worth £255m (€300m) for Ukraine's fight against Russia and was awarded Ukraine's Order of Freedom.Asked if he was concerned about changes of leadership in Britain, and in France next year, Zelensky said: "Of course I'm afraid of changes, of course we are afraid because we are in the war each day."But again the priority is the relation between nations, not just between just people. I'm sure that these relations will not change, or we have to do our best not to lose such very good relations."He added: "I hope we will never lose strong relations with the UK during or after the war." Sir Keir replied: "You won't."Burnham told the BBC in his first major interview since becoming prime minister: "My support for Ukraine is unwavering - it is 100%. And I will do what, in Ukraine, people think is the right thing that they need."He also paid tribute to Sir Keir's "huge personal support" for Zelensky, adding: "He will get exactly the same from me."

schema.headline: Andy Burnham pledges continued support for Ukraine ahead of Zelensky visit

title: Would you choose £50,000 over the chance of £1m?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByCost of living correspondentYou have the choice of instantly receiving £50,000 or flipping a coin for a 50/50 chance of £1
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByCost of living correspondentYou have the choice of instantly receiving £50,000 or flipping a coin for a 50/50 chance of £1m.Which would you choose?The vast majority decide on taking the £50k, according to a survey of thousands of people by YouGov. Women voted 82% in favour of the guaranteed cash.The poll has sparked a debate about why Brits appear more risk-averse than people in the US.So why are the results so clear-cut, and what are the financial and psychological factors at play? Sadly, there is little chance of ever having such a choice, but there are some interesting lessons for how we manage our money nonetheless.Do you agree with the majority?Does the choice depend on how much you earn?Lots of people might opt for the £50,000 guarantee, deciding that it is a life-changing amount of money in itself.After all, it is £10,000 more than the median average earnings for full-time workers in the UK for an entire year, according to official statistics, external.But younger people generally earn less and yet, according to this survey, external, those aged 18 to 24 are more willing to take the bet on £1m than any other age group.Some 28% go for the coin flip, compared with just 11% among the over-65s - their grandparents' generation.There is a different tipping point for everyone. Repeat the survey but instead guarantee £5 or offer a 50/50 chance for a £100, and most people will probably go for the £100 bet. After all, lots of people bet at least £2 a week hoping for a National Lottery win.As those amounts rise, so your appetite for risk becomes clear.Why not just invest the £50k?One choice is to take the guaranteed £50,000 and hope it grows over time. Saving the money would be helped by the magic of compound interest.Alternatively, you could take more of a risk, but potentially with greater reward, by investing the money.What has happened in the past will not necessarily happen in the future when it comes to investments.But you'd have had to have invested your £50,000 in a typical global fund just under 38 years ago for it to be worth £1m today, according to Sarah Coles, of investment firm AJ Bell.Is it all in the mind?We are hardwired, says Coles, to go for the guaranteed £50,000.That's because we feel losses more acutely than gains, she says. "The thrill of potentially winning £1m is felt less strongly than the fear of giving up a guaranteed £50,000 and ending up with nothing," she says.In other words, having £50k and knowing you might have won £1m will play on your mind.But it is not as bad as having a crack at £1m and knowing you've given up enough for an average deposit to buy a home in the West Midlands, external.

schema.headline: Would you choose £50,000 over the chance of £1m?

title: World Matchplay darts 2026 results: Luke Littler defends title and smashes Phil Taylor's average record
description: Luke Littler defended his World Matchplay title in sensational style - and smashed Phil Taylor's tournament and final average records in the process.T
body: Luke Littler defended his World Matchplay title in sensational style - and smashed Phil Taylor's tournament and final average records in the process.The 19-year-old beat seventh seed Gerwyn Price 18-9 in Blackpool to become just the fourth person to win back-to-back Matchplay titles.World number one Littler finished the week with an average of 111.04, beating Taylor's record of 106.31 in 2010. He averaged 111.53 in the final, setting a new record as he bettered Taylor's 111.23 against Adrian Lewis in 2013.Littler claimed £225,000 in prize money for winning the event and now has £3,143,500 over the PDC's two-year order of merit. That is £2.13m more than Luke Humphries in second spot."It's been a crazy week, one of the best weeks of my life with the darts I've played," Littler told Sky Sports."It's been tough. The stats may look like it's easy, but when you're on this stage with how hot it is, it's not easy."Price averaged 104.97 in the final and has enjoyed a successful week, climbing to fourth in the order of merit and reclaiming the Welsh number one spot from Jonny Clayton.Littler went into the final as the overwhelming favourite and a stunning 167 finish in the fourth leg secured an early break to help him claim the first mini-session 4-1.That form continued as he led 8-2 and was averaging 114.74, with Taylor's record of 114.99 in any Matchplay game in sight.His level dropped slightly in the next two sessions, but he still claimed both 3-2 to push ever closer to the finish line.He moved to within two legs with another brilliant 148 checkout - his sixth ton-plus finish in the final - before a break and hold saw him claim his fourth ranking title of the calendar year.The back-to-back world champion also hit 12 180s in the final to set a new tournament record of 66, surpassing the total he set last year.The run is also continuing his sublime form in longer-format matches - this win extending the streak to 29 successive wins in games with 20 or more legs.His last defeat over a match of that duration was when he burst on to the scene in the 2024 World Championship and lost to Luke Humphries in the final."Luke is one in a million, I threw everything at him," Price told Sky Sports."He's fantastic for the sport. I wish he wasn't as good as he is - I would have won a couple more tournaments."I hope there's no-one else like him coming through because he's ridiculous!"Speaking after the final, Little reiterated his intention now was to try to claim a clean sweep of the PDC ranking titles in the calendar year - a feat never achieved before.The Players Championship Finals in November are a sticking point.It would mean needing to play in, and probably win, some Pro Tour events, and Littler has skipped the first 24 and has already pulled out of the two in Hildesheim this week.That leaves just eight left for him to feature in Minehead. A total of 64 players qualify for that event and the final player currently has £22,750 in prize money.A win is worth £15,000 and a runner-up spot £10,000, so Littler has some work to do."I don't think my dad's too happy because we were going to go to Spain and I think we've got to go to Leicester now and play some Pro Tours, but it is what it is," Littler added on Sky Sports."I've been checking the Pro Tour rankings and whoever is in 64th just keeps going up and up and up. I know there are four in Leicester that I've got to go to now and we'll see what happens."If I don't qualify then I'm going to get grilled and if I do, I'll get grilled anyway. Who knows what's going to happen?"Former BDO world champion Mark Webster said he "half expects" the teenager to achieve the clean sweep."Who is going to stop Luke Littler?" he added."You could argue the first round of the Grand Prix because of the short format [best of three sets], but Gian van Veen threw everything at him last year and he had all the answers."At the minute his game just holds up in any format and scenario. He wants to break records. You definitely wouldn't rule it out."

schema.headline: World Matchplay darts 2026 results: Luke Littler defends title and smashes Phil Taylor's average record

title: Israeli settlers set fire to mosques, cars and farm land in West Bank, Palestinians say
description: Israeli settlers have set fire to two mosques, as well as cars and agricultural land in the occupied West Bank, Palestinian officials say, as tensions
body: Israeli settlers have set fire to two mosques, as well as cars and agricultural land in the occupied West Bank, Palestinian officials say, as tensions in the territory continue to flare. The latest attacks come two days after a clash between settlers and Palestinians near the village of Tal, which left four Palestinians and two Israelis dead.Both sides accused the other of provoking the violence. The confrontation has further inflamed the situation in the West Bank, which has seen ever growing violence by extremist settlers against Palestinians, encouraged by far-right elements in the current Israeli government.Palestinian reports say that two villages in the occupied West Bank came under attack from settlers overnight, with cars vandalised, property stolen and hate graffiti spray painted on walls.The mayor of Qusra said that settlers set fire to a mosque that was under construction.Abdul Azim Wadi said that settlers spray painted graffiti that included the word "revenge" on the walls of the mosque.The Israeli military has said that troops were sent to Qusra and that police would investigate and collect evidence.Palestinian officials say that in a separate incident, settlers set fire to another mosque in the village of Kour and sprayed slogans on its walls.Since the deadly clash on Friday in Tal, Palestinians say that there have been multiple settler attacks on villages across the West Bank.The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) has carried out raids and arrested more than 130 individuals over the weekend in what it has called a "counter-terrorism" operation.The Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu responded to the incident in Tal by vowing to take "powerful action".That includes the possible demolition of the homes of two of the Palestinians who were allegedly involved.Kaied Ahmad Turabi, from Miami, was visiting his parents and sister in the village when the attack happened. He was filmed fighting with settlers on a neighbour's porch.He was just out of hospital when he spoke to the BBC. He had a large black eye, several cuts and bruises, and a wound on his head that he said had needed 12 stitches."I worked all my life with Jewish people, but these people... they all had covered faces, all of them had a lot of stuff – sticks, and things in their pockets. They came ready," he said.Hours later, we were with residents watching the back entrance to the village when settlers were spotted on its outskirts again.We watched dozens of young men stream up the road, answering a call to barricade and defend the village.Israeli soldiers stood guard to separate the groups, as the settlers slowly melted away.For the Palestinians, it was a different method of crowd control - tear gas fired repeatedly to push them back down the road.Some young men ran through clouds of gas to try and bury the cannisters with soil, or kick them away to chants of "Palestine, Palestine", as the soldiers steadily advanced.Israel's military said on Sunday it was working to prevent "incidents of nationalist crime" - its term for attacks by extremist Israeli settlers there.But while Israeli leaders publicly condemn extremist violence, they have overseen a rapid growth in the wildcat settlement outposts that human rights groups say are fuelling attacks on Palestinians.Israel's prime minister said he would speed up the establishment and legalisation of farm outposts in the West Bank, in response to the killing of Israelis in Tal on Friday.New Israeli outposts have already appeared in the area since then - one near Sarra is visible from the main road.There has been a sharp increase in settler attacks in the West Bank in recent months.It has drawn international condemnation, but shown little or no sign of being reversed.The situation had already deteriorated before the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on October 7, 2023.But since the subsequent war waged by Israel against Hamas in Gaza erupted, settler violence in the West Bank has escalated.The UN says 1,114 Palestinians have been killed in the West Bank, the vast majority by the IDF. It says at least 35 of the deaths have involved attacks by settlers.It says 41 Israelis, including civilians and security personnel, have been killed in Palestinian attacks or during Israeli military operations in the West Bank since the start of the Gaza war.Israel has built hundreds of settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem - land Palestinians want, along with Gaza, for a hoped-for future state - during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them. The settlements are illegal under international law.

schema.headline: Israeli settlers set fire to mosques, cars and farm land in West Bank, Palestinians say

title: Newspaper headlines: Youth benefits 'crack down' and Gatwick 'Fly and dry'
description: The i Paper, external says Andy Burnham is "actively considering" replacing stamp duty and council tax. It says the options being mooted as replacemen
body: The i Paper, external says Andy Burnham is "actively considering" replacing stamp duty and council tax. It says the options being mooted as replacements are a land value tax and a proportional property tax, which would be 0.48% of a home's value each year. The paper says the chancellor will make a decision in the run-up to the budget. The Daily Telegraph, external also claims it has a glimpse into the new thinking in Downing Street. It says young people will be stripped of their benefits unless they agree to do training or voluntary work, as part of a government plan to reduce the benefits bill. The paper says the aim is to find savings to fund defence spending.The Daily Mail, external focuses on Wes Streeting's comment that he would hypothetically resign as defence secretary, at some point in the future, if he felt that his department wasn't sufficiently funded. The paper's editorial questions whether defence funding is above social care in Number 10's priorities. The Guardian's, external lead is that the new foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, will be taking up a role on the board of the World Bank, usually given to a junior minister, which would place international aid as a foreign policy priority.The Financial Times, external says the world's biggest defence companies are investing billions of pounds into small start-ups in the sector. It says it is to benefit from tech advancements in the face of increased government spending on defence. The Daily Mirror, external says finance campaigners are lobbying Number 10 to impose new taxes on banks. It comes as half-year results are to be declared in the next fortnight and are likely to show record profits.The Daily Star, external has found that almost 800 people a day, on average, are driving away from petrol stations without paying. It says the figure has doubled over a 12-month period and is based on a freedom of information (FOI) request from the paper. The FOI response shows the DVLA was contacted 290,000 times for the registered keeper of a vehicle, in the 2025-26 financial year.The Sun, external splashes with an exclusive that Cristiano Ronaldo is producing, and will appear in, a drama about football that is partly being filmed in Barnet, in north London. The series is called "Day Ones" and depicts the fictional life of a football agent. An insider tells the Sun it's a "prestige project".

schema.headline: Newspaper headlines: Youth benefits 'crack down' and Gatwick 'Fly and dry'

title: Tour de France 2026: Tadej Pogacar wins fifth Tour as Mathieu van der Poel takes stage 21
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Tadej Pogacar is considered one of the greatest riders of all timeByMatt WarwickBBC Sport Senior JournalistSl
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Tadej Pogacar is considered one of the greatest riders of all timeByMatt WarwickBBC Sport Senior JournalistSlovenian Tadej Pogacar won the Tour de France for a record-equalling fifth time.The 27-year-old UAE Team Emirates-XRG rider crossed the line on Paris' Champs-Elysees in the peloton, to join Jacques Anquetil, Eddy Merckx, Bernard Hinault and Miguel Indurain as the endurance event's most successful male riders.All-conquering Pogacar raised the idea that his remarkable reality is proving stranger than fiction, describing it as "something you wouldn't even maybe write in a story book".The three-week Grand Tour's final stage was won by the Netherlands' Mathieu van der Poel of Alpecin-Premier Tech after a frantic charge to the line on the French capital's famous cobbles in which he pipped team-mate Jasper Philipsen of Belgium by inches.Pogacar's victory means he is positioned by many as the greatest cyclist of all time, superseding the achievements and status of Belgian legend Merckx.It also marks Pogacar's third Tour win in succession and includes a record-breaking ascent of the iconic Alpe d'Huez on stage 19, when he sealed another dominant victory.It was the last of five stage wins in a race in which Pogacar used his explosive launch and unmatchable metronomic pace to see off his rivals, who for some time have had virtually no answer.Pogacar has won almost every major race in the sport, including the Tour of Flanders, Giro d'Italia, Milan-San Remo, Road World Championships, Giro di Lombardia and Liege-Bastogne-Liege.Pogacar was booed by some fans during the Tour, as his performances are often so far ahead of any of his peers that some feel frustrated the sport is losing its competitive edge.He now has 127 wins in an eight-year elite professional career."Victory is really special," said Pogacar. "Thank you to all the fans and my team."But the biggest thanks goes to all my family who support me all my life. My parents - without them I would not be standing here five times already."Seven Tours and seven times on the podium, and five wins, is something you wouldn't even maybe write in a story book, and it's unbelievable for me."It's a magnificent podium with some incredible champions to fight with."It's a shame Jonas [Vingegaard] crashed out this time and many others. I hope they have a quick recovery and next year we fight again."High drama on the Champs-ElyseesThe famous final stage, which for the overall contenders is an unchallenged formality, typically becomes a flat bunch sprint.Last year organisers ASO introduced a circuit which takes on a cobbled climb over the city's famous Montmartre hill, changing the parcours enough to encourage the heavier, more powerful riders to challenge for victory.On Sunday it was powerhouse classics legend Van der Poel who took victory after charging away with 11km remaining with Pogacar.Pogacar and Van der Poel led through the picturesque and narrow lanes over Montmartre and past Sacre-Coeur, where some fans had mobile phones knocked out of their hands as the riders squeezed past at speed, before Pogacar began to fade after three weeks of dominance and showing no weakness.Van der Poel, whose strength and staying power allow him to pull out gaps in gruelling one-day races, just managed to stay ahead of a chasing pack which included several sprinters and was rapidly closing, before he crossed the line, collapsed off his bike and lay under a barrier, breathing heavily for several minutes.Van der Poel added this prestigious victory on the famous cobbles to many of the sport's biggest one-day races, such as multiple victories in Paris-Roubaix and the Tour of Flanders.He said: "We have a saying in Dutch that it has to come for your toes. I don't know where this came from, but not from my toes."The stage was reduced from 133km to 89km after the redirection of emergency services to help tackle wildfires in south-west France.Image gallerySkip image galleryImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Pogacar leads the peloton past the Arc de TriompheSlide 1 of 5, Tadej Pogacar rides past the Arc de Triomphe, Pogacar leads the peloton past the Arc de TriompheA future beyond Pogacar?The one rider who has broken Pogacar's stranglehold of cycling's biggest race in the past was Denmark's Vingegaard, who won in 2022 and 2023.But this year the 29-year-old Visma-Lease a Bike rider abandoned after breaking his collarbone on a easy right-hand bend on stage 15.The mistake was very unlike Vingegaard's near perfect technique and execution as a rider, and attention soon turned to scrutiny of the International Testing Agency (ITA), which had awoken Vingegaard at 2am to carry out an anti-doping test.Other riders had the same treatment, including Pogacar at 5am, but the ITA said there was "exceptional circumstances" to take the night tests, which are rare and require additional permission.It is not known when the test results will be published.Pogacar's only other real rival was the much-improved Belgian Remco Evenepoel of Red Bull-Bora-Hansgohe, who finished six minutes 26 seconds behind overall.Third place went to Pogacar's Mexican team-mate Isaac del Toro, who won stage two thanks largely to Pogacar's babysitting pace in the lead-up to the line.It would not be the only time Pogacar would aid Del Toro, 22, sacrificing his own potential victory on Saturday's brutal 'queen' stage to Alpe d'Huez to consolidate Del Toro's place on the podium.Del Toro's white jersey for the best young rider came at the expense of France's new 19-year-old star Paul Seixas of Decathlon-CMA CGM. Seixas looked stronger than Del Toro at times on the climbs but faded substantially on Saturday.Many think Seixas will be a rival to Pogacar in the future.Pidcock pleased but Netcompany without a winIn the year when Britain's four-time Tour winner Chris Froome retired, his former team - now known as Netcompany Ineos Cycling - failed to record a stage victory in 21 attempts.Ex-Ineos rider Tom Pidcock of Pinarello-Q36.5 won on Alpe d'Huez four years ago and returned to this race having achieved much with a new team built entirely around him.The 26-year-old did not manage to win a stage, but he and his team will be satisfied with Pidcock's consistent battling riding, which earned him ninth in the general classification to build on third place in last year's Vuelta a Espana.Fellow Briton Adam Yates, 33, showed great tenacity after falling ill on stage 16 and spending two days riding at the back of the field before helping pace Pogacar up a climb for victory on stage 19.Who won which jerseys?One of the most entertaining riders in the race was Ecuador's Richard Carapaz of EF Education-Easypost. He toiled earlier in the race before coming into great form to claim the king of the mountains' polka dot jersey.  He won stage 18 and Saturday's stage 20 after topping the race's highest point first and after 5,450km of climbing.The green points jersey was awarded to Denmark's Mads Pedersen of Lidl-Trek, after tenacious riding on climbs he is not typically strong on to hoover up mid-stage points, alongside winning stage four.He beat a number of sprinters to the jersey, including Philipsen of Alpecin-Premier Tech. Philipsen won stage 17 and fellow Belgian Tim Merlier of Soudal-Quick Step won three bunch sprint stages.Tour de France stage 21 results1. title: Morgan Rogers: Chelsea boss Xabi Alonso has 'plan' for record signing to play alongside Cole Palmer
description: Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso says he has a "plan" to play club record £117m signing Morgan Rogers alongside Cole Palmer - and believes the England inte
body: Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso says he has a "plan" to play club record £117m signing Morgan Rogers alongside Cole Palmer - and believes the England international will make an "instant impact".The midfielder became the most expensive British player of all-time when he moved from Aston Villa to Stamford Bridge last week.The 24-year-old is on holiday after playing for England at the World Cup, while Chelsea have begun their pre-season tour in Sydney."In that position we needed an important player and I'm sure there were not many better options than Morgan Rogers," Alonso said."You need players who can have that almost instant impact and I'm sure Morgan won't need much time to adapt to the club, the system and his team-mates," Alonso said."That was the idea, to get a top player, and Morgan is one of them."Rogers has signed a six-year contract with Chelsea, with an option for a further year.Alonso insisted he will be ready, despite not yet taking part in pre-season training, and believes he will be compatible with fellow England international Palmer.The pair describe each other as being among their "best friends in football", with Rogers saying they would love to play together."I have a plan. I have an idea. I can see them linking really well," Alonso said of the pair."We need to have a good mix. If we get that balance right and those special players in the right positions, with good control, then we will be more competitive with and without the ball."The Blues are also expected to announce the £52m signing of France international defender Maxence Lacroix from Crystal Palace.The 26-year-old would be Chelsea's oldest signing since 2022."We want a squad with the right balance between quality and mentality," Alonso said."Those things need to match in terms of maturity, but I think we are starting the new season with good energy. That's important."Chelsea have also brought in winger Geovany Quenda from Sporting, striker Emmanuel Emegha from Strasbourg and full-back Marco Palestra from Atalanta, and are expected to sign midfielder Valentin Barco, also from Strasbourg, in the coming weeks.That will leave Chelsea with nearly 40 players in their squad and needing to sell a substantial number of them."We need to know that there will probably still be some movement," Alonso added."We need to be flexible and quick to act. The main thing is that we have a clear idea, a clear plan that we have built. "It will probably change before the transfer window closes."

schema.headline: Morgan Rogers: Chelsea boss Xabi Alonso has 'plan' for record signing to play alongside Cole Palmer

title: Water returns to Gatwick Airport after major outage
description: Gatwick Airport says its water supply has returned after passengers faced long queues for toilets and closed restaurants and bars after a major supply
body: Gatwick Airport says its water supply has returned after passengers faced long queues for toilets and closed restaurants and bars after a major supply outage.Both terminals at the UK's second busiest airport lost running water on Sunday morning after a power failure at a treatment works that serves the area.People told the BBC of confusion and frustration as all bars and restaurants were shut, some were left with nowhere to sit and waits built up outside toilets.SES Water, the company that supplies the airport, said earlier the power outage was fixed, with Gatwick reporting on Sunday night that water had returned to "the vast majority of the London Gatwick campus".The water company, which also supplies parts of Kent, Surrey and south London, said complications caused by a power outage at Bough Beech treatment works meant some customers had experienced low water pressure or a temporary loss of supply.A spokesperson had earlier confirmed that Gatwick Airport was affected.On Sunday afternoon, SES Water said its treatment works were back up and running, but later added it would take time for the network to fully return to normal as it had been "a highly unusual and complex issue"."We want to reiterate that our teams are working as quickly as they possibly can and we are grateful for everyone's patience," the spokesperson added.Gatwick apologised and said staff had been handing out bottled water.A spokesperson added: "Our staff are on hand to support passengers and provide assistance where needed, some restaurant partners have opened to provide additional seating."Gatwick said additional teams had been deployed across both terminals to support passengers.The airport added there had been no flight cancellations as a result of the supply issues and that it was working closely with SES Water to minimise the impact."Our teams are working hard to reopen toilets and other facilities as quickly and safely as possible," a spokesperson said.BBC reporter Adam Dowling, who was flying from Valencia to Gatwick, said his flight had been delayed because of the water supply disruption and passengers had been informed that landing slots were being moved around "to reduce the number of flights" coming in to Gatwick.The BBC has contacted Gatwick Airport to confirm if there has been any flight disruption.Roger Wood, from Tunbridge Wells in Kent, said he thought his friends were joking when they told him there were no restaurants or bars open in Gatwick's south terminal.When he arrived to meet them ahead of his flight on Sunday, he found "there was no water at all - no Nando's, no Wetherspoon, all of those places were completely shut and stopping people coming in as there was no fresh water or ability to wash hands".Wood told the BBC: "The only place you could buy something was places like Pret and Itsu where it was packaged food, or shops."There was a general grumpiness and the usual frustration at not being able to get a drink at a bar from people, but everybody seemed quite resigned."Wood said people could go in the toilets but there was no way to wash hands and conditions had grown worse in the hour or two they were there.Houchin said there has been "very little information" from the airport."I think people are just fed up because they've got a long wait, but everyone understands there's nothing you can do about it," she added.Ian Bubb, who was flying to Alicante in Spain with British Airways, said there had been a "total lack of information" from the airport."Absolute disgrace at Gatwick - total lack of contingency planning for such an event," he said.The passenger said he had booked a lounge but was not allowed to sit inside.People heading to the airport for flights have been advised not to arrive early.A statement from Easyjet said: "Due to a water supply issue affecting London Gatwick Airport, bag drop desks are temporarily opening two hours before departure instead of three hours."The airline said: "Please do not arrive earlier, as you will not be able to drop off your bags or enter the departure lounge until bag drop opens."SES Water confirmed the Kent postcodes TN8 and TN11 and parts of Surrey postcodes RH1, RH6 and RH10 had no water supply or low pressure. The company said it was delivering bottled water to vulnerable customers.Gatwick Airport and the local area also suffered water issues in July 2022, when low pressure caused by a burst water main affected 1,200 houses and closed toilet facilities at the airport.

schema.headline: Water returns to Gatwick Airport after major outage

title: It's me, Cathy – thousands pay tribute to Kate Bush classic
description: The sun may be hiding behind grey clouds, but for hundreds of people in flowing red dresses dancing on Yorkshire moorland it'll take more than a threa
body: The sun may be hiding behind grey clouds, but for hundreds of people in flowing red dresses dancing on Yorkshire moorland it'll take more than a threat of rain to dampen their spirits.This is Brontë country, after all, so it's fitting that it's also perfect Brontë weather.The group, swaying in unison, have come together to re-create the music video for Kate Bush's 1978 song Wuthering Heights, inspired by Emily Brontë's novel.Every year, thousands of people around the world don red robes – and in some cases long black wigs – for The Most Wuthering Heights Day Ever.Events have previously taken place in places such as Sydney, Copenhagen, Berlin, Folkestone and Preston.This particular "Mass Wuther" perhaps has an even stronger claim than most – it's held on Penistone Hill, not far from the famous Brontë parsonage in Haworth, in the Pennines.From the field on a clear day can be seen the ruined farmhouse of Top Withens, believed to be the inspiration for the titular farmhouse of Brontë's novel."We're really thrilled to be bringing all these people together. It's such a good-hearted, fun event. It doesn't matter whether you can dance or not," says organiser Lydia McKinnon."I just hope that the Kates and Cathys have got their thermals and their rain ponchos because they might need them."The West Yorkshire event was a sell-out in 2025, and this year the 500 tickets were snapped up within 90 seconds, according to event organisers.Proceeds are split between regional and national charities. This year, Women's Aid, Haworth and Oxenhope District Bridleways Group, and Friends of Brontë Country have been chosen.Some participants in the Mass Wuther have travelled great distances to attend – in the case of Frances Murphy and Katherine Egan, all the way from Australia. They both took part in Brisbane's event last year and said they couldn't miss the opportunity to dance in Brontë Country."It's wonderful. So many people have turned out,  and we're so lucky to have got tickets to get in," Katherine says, adding: "We love you, England."

schema.headline: It's me, Cathy – thousands pay tribute to Kate Bush classic
